raw_case_text:
Six-year-old female child, first product of nonconsanguineous marriage resident of New Delhi, presented with fever for four days, yellowish discoloration of eyes, and urine for two days, progressive swelling of whole body starting from feet for one day. Fever was moderate to high grade, intermittent in type associated with chills and rigor subsided with medication and profuse sweating. She was having high coloured urine for two days. Progressive swelling of whole body for last one day starting from feet then involved the whole body. Stools were normal in colour. There was no history of black coloured stools, vomiting, bleeding from any site, and any change in conscious level, jaundice in the past, any history of blood transfusion, and intravenous medication in the past or any history of drug intake. There was no history suggestive of respiratory tract infections, skin infection, decreased micturition, and reddish coloured urine. There was no significant past, antenatal, perinatal, or family history. The child was fully immunized and was receiving adequate calories and proteins for her age.
On examination, the child was conscious, cooperative, and orientated. At admission her pulse was 78 per minute, respiratory rate 26 per minute, and blood pressure 98/68 mm of mercury. There were severe pallor, and icterus. Lymph nodes were not palpable. On abdominal examination liver was palpable 4 cms below costal margin with span of 10 cm the spleen was palpable 1 cms below costal margin. Her respiratory, cardiovascular (CVS), and central nervous system (CNS) examination was unremarkable.
On investigation haemoglobin was 4.9 g/dL, total leucocyte count 10.6 x 103 per muL with polymorphs 54%, lymphocytes 42%, monocyte 4%, platelet count 11x103 per muL and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 8 mm/1st hour by Westergren method. Blood sugar was 84 mg/dL. Total serum bilirubin was 27.5 mg/dL, indirect fraction of 18 mg/dL. SGOT was 495 and SGPT 210. Serum total protein was 2.8 gram (gm) and albumin 1 gm per 100 mL of blood. Blood urea nitrogen was 189 mg/dL, creatinine 0.6 mg/dL, sodium 136 meq/L, potassium 4.1 meq/L. Prothrombin time was 17.3/12 with INR of 1.44. Viral markers (HBsAg, IgM hepatitis C, A and E) were negative. Chest X-ray was normal and ultrasonography abdomen showed hepatosplenomegaly. On peripheral smear trophozoites and schizonts of P. vivax and trophozoites and gametocytes of P. falciparum were seen. Rapid malarial antigen test was positive. Arterial blood gas analysis showed pH 7.45, partial pressure (PP) of oxygen 104, PP of carbon dioxide 45, and standard bicarbonate 28 meq/L. Urine routine and microscopy were normal. She was given injection of Artesunate 2.4 gm per kilogram body weight, along with cefotaxime and vitamin K. She received fresh frozen plasma, packed red cell, platelets along with inotropes. Within five hours of admission she developed profuse upper gastrointestinal bleeding, along with deterioration of consciousness. She went into shock, then cardiorespiratory arrest from which she could not be revived.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 6-year-old female presenting with fever for four days, jaundice for two days, and generalized body swelling for one day.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 6-year-old girl presented with a four-day history of intermittent moderate-to-high grade fever associated with chills, rigors, and profuse diaphoresis, which temporarily subsided with antipyretics. Two days prior to presentation, she developed progressive yellowish discoloration of her eyes and dark-colored urine. One day prior, she developed rapidly progressive generalized edema (anasarca) beginning in the lower extremities and involving the entire body. Stools remained normal in color. There was no history of melena, hematemesis, epistaxis, altered consciousness, oliguria, or red urine. Within five hours of hospital admission, she developed catastrophic upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage, progressive shock, and cardiac arrest.
subjective.past_medical_history: First child of non-consanguineous marriage, resident of New Delhi. Fully immunized for age, adequate nutritional intake. No history of jaundice, blood transfusions, intravenous medications, or prior hospitalizations. Unremarkable antenatal, perinatal, and family history.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, chills, rigors, diaphoresis, jaundice, dark urine, and progressive generalized swelling (anasarca). Negative for cough, dyspnea, skin infection, hematuria, oliguria, vomiting, hematochezia, or altered sensorium on admission. Medications: antipyretics for fever. Allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Conscious, cooperative, and oriented on admission. Pulse rate 78 beats/min, respiratory rate 26 breaths/min, blood pressure 98/68 mmHg. Severe pallor, deep icterus, and generalized anasarca present. No peripheral lymphadenopathy. Abdominal examination: tender hepatomegaly palpable 4 cm below the costal margin (liver span 10 cm); splenomegaly palpable 1 cm below the costal margin. Respiratory, cardiovascular, and central nervous system examinations were normal on admission. Terminal examination at 5 hours: massive hematemesis, altered consciousness, unrecordable blood pressure (shock), and cardiorespiratory arrest.
objective.routine_investigations: Hemoglobin 4.9 g/dL, total leukocyte count 10.6 x 10^3/muL (polymorphs 54%, lymphocytes 42%, monocytes 4%), platelets 11 x 10^3/muL (severe thrombocytopenia), ESR 8 mm/1st hr (Westergren). Blood glucose 84 mg/dL. Total serum bilirubin 27.5 mg/dL (indirect fraction 18 mg/dL). AST/SGOT 495 U/L, ALT/SGPT 210 U/L. Total serum protein 2.8 g/dL, serum albumin 1.0 g/dL. Blood urea nitrogen 189 mg/dL, creatinine 0.6 mg/dL, sodium 136 mEq/L, potassium 4.1 mEq/L. Coagulation: prothrombin time 17.3/12 sec, INR 1.44. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.45, PaO2 104 mmHg, PaCO2 45 mmHg, standard bicarbonate 28 mEq/L. Urinalysis: normal routine and microscopy. Viral hepatitis serologies (HBsAg, IgM anti-HCV, IgM anti-HAV, IgM anti-HEV): all negative. Chest X-ray: normal. Bedside abdominal ultrasound: hepatosplenomegaly. Peripheral blood smear performed.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe mixed Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium falciparum malaria complicated by profound hemolytic anemia (hemoglobin 4.9 g/dL), severe thrombocytopenia (11,000/muL), extreme hyperbilirubinemia (total bilirubin 27.5 mg/dL), severe hypoalbuminemia with anasarca, prerenal azotemia (BUN 189 mg/dL), coagulopathy (INR 1.44), massive upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage, and fatal shock.
Diagnostic confirmation: Peripheral blood smear demonstrating trophozoites and schizonts of Plasmodium vivax along with trophozoites and gametocytes of Plasmodium falciparum; positive rapid malarial antigen test; negative acute viral hepatitis serologies (HAV, HBV, HCV, HEV).
Treatment & Outcome: Managed urgently with intravenous artesunate (2.4 mg/kg), IV cefotaxime, intravenous vitamin K, transfusions of fresh frozen plasma, packed red blood cells, and platelets, along with inotropic support. Despite intensive resuscitation, the patient developed profuse upper gastrointestinal bleeding within five hours of admission, rapidly deteriorated into refractory shock, and suffered cardiorespiratory arrest with unsuccessful resuscitation.
